title: seller-sparring-guide-llm-endpoints-strategic-angles
content:
Purpose: a tactical sparring guide for sellers and solution engineers to (a) quickly map customer needs to Redwood’s strongest defenses vs general LLM API providers, (b) anticipate common traps and commit to measured claims, and (c) run 3 realistic role‑play scenarios that expose feature gaps and let reps win the conversation without overpromising.

Audience: field sellers, solutions engineers, AE managers, and pre-sales engineers running technical discovery calls with product and infra teams.

High-level positioning thesis (one-liners you can say quickly):
- We help teams move from ‘model access’ to ‘predictable inference in production’ — that means consistent latency, cost control, and rollout safety across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- If their ask is purely model access on a credit card, Redwood is sometimes more than they need — but when customers talk SLAs, data isolation, or unit economics at scale, that’s where we win.

Three core messaging pillars (use in this order during discovery):
1) Predictable economics: explain batching, caching, and dedicated capacity as levers to reduce per-token cost without sacrificing latency SLOs. Ask: "What does a 2–3x change in token volume do to your bill and latency today?"
2) Operational safety: rollouts, canaries, automatic fallbacks, and model pinning reduce the blast radius of model regressions. Ask: "How do you currently detect and rollback a model quality regression in production?"
3) Deployment flexibility: same API surface for hosted, reserved, and private deployments — lowers engineering lift and compliance friction. Ask: "Do you need VPC/private control plane or KMS/HSM today or in the near future?"

Feature comparison shorthand (for quick call notes): (use conservative language; avoid naming specific competitor limitations as absolute unless validated)
- Latency predictability: Redwood: high (dedicated GPU pools + smart routing + autoscaling policies); Generic LLM API: variable (shared pools, queuing spikes).
- Cost controls: Redwood: batching/caching suggestions + reserved capacity options + per-route cost breakdowns; Generic LLM API: price per token with limited unit-cost levers.
- Rollouts & safety: Redwood: A/B, canary, automatic fallback, model pinning; Generic LLM API: limited rollout primitives or manual versioning.
- Private deployment: Redwood: VPC + on-prem package + KMS/HSM integrations; Generic LLM API: limited or no on-prem offerings.
- Observability: Redwood: token-level traces, per-route latency/cost dashboards, regressions tied to evals; Generic LLM API: request logs and metrics but less integrated quality tooling.

Real objections and high‑impact rebuttals (short scripts):
Objection: "We can just self-host an open model and save money."
- Rebuttal: "Many teams start there and hit operational drag: latency spikes, KV cache management, and rollout sprawl. Redwood packages the serving runtime + orchestration so you get predictable latency and SRE-grade rollout tooling without building the ops layer from scratch. If you want, we can walk through a three-month TCO comparison for your expected qps and sequence lengths."

Objection: "Pricing looks higher than the bare‑metal per-token cost I saw."
- Rebuttal: "The per-token number alone misses unit economics: Redwood reduces waste with prefix caching and batching, which often lowers your effective cost per meaningful token. We can run a quick pilot to show end-to-end cost for your workload mix (chat vs bulk embed vs reranking)."

Objection: "We’re already on a competitor and migrating is risky."
- Rebuttal: "We design migrations around compatibility — same API surface and fallback policies. Start with a non-critical route (internal tooling or low-volume feature) and use our canary rollouts plus automated fallbacks; you’ll get comparable results with a smaller blast radius."

Common traps to avoid (coaching for reps):
- Trap: price-only conversations — steer back to predictable TCO, latency SLOs, and operational risk.
- Trap: feature laundry lists — rather than reciting every bullet, map 2–3 feature hooks to the buyer’s risk profile (cost, compliance, latency).
- Trap: exaggerating performance gains — use conservative numbers and offer to run a scoped pilot; claim ’typical’ improvements not guarantees.

Golden discovery questions (to surface competitive weakness):
- "What’s your worst-case latency spike in the last 90 days and what caused it?"
- "How do you measure per-request inference cost today and where does it show up on your bill?"
- "Who owns rollbacks when a new model variant causes regressions? How long does a rollback take?"
- "What constraints would force you to need a private deployment? List security, legal, or latency reasons."

Role-play scenarios (3):
1) Platform Lead (complicated SLOs): 30m call scenario — the lead is worried about 99th percentile latency. Playbook: open with latency distribution question, illustrate smart routing and dedicated capacity, commit to a perf baseline pilot with real sequences. Close: offer an infra-level tech deep dive.
2) Growth PM (cost-sensitive): 25m call scenario — the PM wants to scale embeddings and minimize cost. Playbook: ask about query mix and reuse patterns, explain batching and caching, offer an A/B pilot comparing effective per-embedding cost. Close: propose a 6‑8 week pilot with a cost dashboard.
3) Security/Compliance Manager (private deploy): 40m call scenario — concerned about data residency and key management. Playbook: surface KMS/HSM needs, explain private control plane and audit logs, show SOC/compliance artifacts. Close: propose an NDA + architecture review and timeline for a proof-of-concept VPC deploy.

Call artifacts to leave behind (post-call deliverables):
- Short one-pager mapping their top 3 risks to Redwood features (<=1 page).
- Pilot proposal with success metrics (SLOs, cost delta, timeline).
- Link to a sample deployment runbook and rollback playbook.

Data and claim hygiene (mandatory for reps):
- Don’t promise % cost savings without a scoped pilot. If asked for numbers, use phrasing: "based on similar customers, we typically see X–Y% effective cost improvement after we enable prefix caching and tuning".
- Ask for sample request distributions before committing to kernel-level performance claims.
- If a competitor feature is alleged, ask for a short demo or doc before asserting it’s missing.

Win / Loss signals to track (for AE managers):
- Win signals: commitment to a pilot with production traffic, request for dedicated capacity pricing, security review kickoff.
- Loss signals: conversation stuck on raw token price, procurement asks for purely price comparisons with no performance SLAs, or buyer insists on long-term self-host timeline.

Calibration notes for SEs:
- When asked deep technical questions about kernel selection, be honest about the tradeoffs (quantization vs throughput vs latency). Offer a deep-dive session with Serving Runtime eng if they ask.
- If they want microbenchmarks, request an anonymized trace and propose a short benchmark run on our Dedicated infra.

Appendix: sample closing email (send within 24h)
Subject: Next steps + pilot outline for <customer-name>
Hi <name>,
Thanks for the discussion today — summary below and next steps.
1) Top risks you mentioned: 99th percentile latency spikes, embedding unit-cost, audit/KMS requirement.
2) What Redwood will do: propose a 6‑week pilot on a dedicated pool with prefix caching enabled and canary rollouts; we’ll instrument a cost/latency dashboard and hand off a rollback playbook.
3) Proposed next step: NDA + architecture review + scoped pilot proposal by EOD week.
I’m attaching a 1‑page mapping doc and the pilot outline.
Best,
<AE name>

This doc is meant to be lightweight and actionable — update quarterly with new pilot wins and any validated competitor moves. Keep an internal copy with call notes and pilot outcomes linked to JIRA tickets.

Quick update checklist for this doc (owner: Priya):
- After each lost deal: add a short note on why the buyer focused on price or other non-technical constraints.
- After every pilot: record effective cost delta and latency P99 delta.
- Quarterly: add new rebuttals for emerging competitors.

End of guide.
